sec-fc-01.front: What takes precedence in IAM when both an Allow and an explicit Deny apply?
sec-fc-01.back: Explicit Deny always wins. If there is no Allow at all, the default is implicit deny.

sec-fc-02.back: Sets the maximum permissions an IAM user/role can have. It does not grant permissions on its own; effective permissions are the intersection with the identity policy.

sec-fc-03.front: An application on EC2 needs to call AWS APIs: what to use instead of access keys?
sec-fc-03.back: An IAM role attached via an instance profile; the application gets temporary credentials from instance metadata (IMDSv2 recommended).

sec-fc-04.front: Best practices for the root user?
sec-fc-04.back: Enable MFA, do not create access keys (delete any that exist), use root only for tasks that require it; use a separate admin for daily work.

sec-fc-05.front: IAM Access Advisor vs IAM Credential Report
sec-fc-05.back: Access Advisor: which services a user/role last used and when. Credential Report: password, MFA and access key status of every user in the account.

sec-fc-06.front: Do SCPs apply to the management account?
sec-fc-06.back: No. SCPs apply to every principal in member accounts (including the member account root user) but do not affect the management account.

sec-fc-07.back: No. An SCP only sets a maximum limit; an IAM policy Allow is still required to have permissions.

sec-fc-08.back: A condition in resource-based policies (e.g., bucket policy) to allow only principals in your organization, automatically covering new accounts.

sec-fc-09.back: Builds a best-practice multi-account landing zone on Organizations: Log Archive/Audit accounts, Identity Center, preventive (SCP) and detective (Config) controls, Account Factory.

sec-fc-10.front: External ID in a trust policy
sec-fc-10.back: A secret string the third party must pass when calling AssumeRole, used to prevent the confused deputy problem when granting cross-account access to a vendor.

sec-fc-11.front: What can AWS RAM share (exam examples)?
sec-fc-11.back: VPC subnets (VPC sharing), Transit Gateway, Route 53 Resolver rules, License Manager configurations... across accounts, without copying resources.

sec-fc-12.front: Cognito User Pool vs Identity Pool
sec-fc-12.back: User Pool: sign-up/sign-in, returns JWTs. Identity Pool: exchanges tokens for temporary AWS credentials, supports guest access.

sec-fc-13.back: A proxy that forwards authentication requests to on-premises AD, does not store or cache directory data in AWS; requires VPN or Direct Connect.

sec-fc-14.front: When to choose AWS Managed Microsoft AD?
sec-fc-14.back: When you need a real Active Directory on AWS for AD-aware applications (SQL Server, SharePoint) and/or a trust with on-premises AD.

sec-fc-15.back: Samba-based AD-compatible directory, low cost, basic features, does not support trust with other ADs.

sec-fc-16.front: Security Group: stateful or stateless? Does it have Deny?
sec-fc-16.back: Stateful, Allow rules only, applied at the ENI/instance level, can reference other Security Groups.

sec-fc-17.back: Stateless, has Allow and Deny, applied at the subnet level, evaluated by rule number; ephemeral ports must be opened for return traffic.

sec-fc-18.front: How to place NAT Gateways for HA?
sec-fc-18.back: One NAT Gateway in the public subnet of each AZ, with private subnet route tables pointing to the NAT Gateway in the same AZ.

sec-fc-19.front: What special configuration does a NAT instance need?
sec-fc-19.back: Disable source/destination check, place it in a public subnet with a public IP; you manage HA and patching yourself.

sec-fc-20.front: How does Session Manager replace a bastion host?
sec-fc-20.back: Shell access via SSM Agent, no inbound ports, no SSH keys; permissions via IAM, session logs to S3/CloudWatch Logs.

sec-fc-21.front: Do VPC Flow Logs record packet contents?
sec-fc-21.back: No, only metadata (IP, port, protocol, ACCEPT/REJECT). To capture packet contents use Traffic Mirroring.

sec-fc-22.front: Which services does a gateway endpoint support?
sec-fc-22.back: Only Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. Free, works through route tables, not accessible from on-premises.

sec-fc-23.back: An ENI with a private IP in your subnet to reach most AWS services or third-party services; charged per hour and per GB, accessible from on-premises.

sec-fc-24.back: No. Also, the CIDRs of the two VPCs must not overlap. Use Transit Gateway when you need transitive routing.

sec-fc-25.front: Is Direct Connect encrypted by default?
sec-fc-25.back: No. Use IPsec VPN over DX or MACsec on supported connections to encrypt.

sec-fc-26.back: Lets a single Direct Connect connection reach VPCs in multiple Regions (and multiple accounts).

sec-fc-27.back: Multiple branch offices (customer gateways) connect by VPN to the same virtual private gateway and communicate with each other in a hub-and-spoke model.

sec-fc-28.front: AWS managed key vs customer managed key in KMS
sec-fc-28.back: AWS managed: managed by AWS, rotates automatically every year, key policy not editable, cannot be shared cross-account. Customer managed: you control key policy, rotation, cross-account access, disable/delete.

sec-fc-29.back: Use a data key (from GenerateDataKey) to encrypt large data locally, then store the data key encrypted by the KMS key alongside the data. KMS Encrypt directly handles only up to 4 KB.

sec-fc-30.back: CloudHSM: single-tenant HSM, customer has full control of keys, AWS cannot access them. KMS: managed multi-tenant service, deeply integrated with AWS services.

sec-fc-31.front: What is the current default encryption for S3?
sec-fc-31.back: Since January 2023, all new objects are encrypted by default with SSE-S3. Choose SSE-KMS for key auditing/control.

sec-fc-32.front: How to encrypt a running RDS database that is not encrypted?
sec-fc-32.back: Create a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, restore a new DB from the encrypted snapshot, and switch the application to the new DB.

sec-fc-33.front: Object Lock: governance vs compliance mode
sec-fc-33.back: Governance: users with special permission can bypass. Compliance: no one, including root, can delete or shorten retention.

sec-fc-34.back: The customer sends the key with every request; S3 encrypts/decrypts but does not store the key; HTTPS is required.

sec-fc-35.back: Secrets Manager: built-in automatic rotation (RDS, Aurora, Redshift), cross-Region replication, paid. Parameter Store: stores configuration, SecureString, free standard tier, no built-in rotation.

sec-fc-36.front: Which Region must an ACM certificate for CloudFront be in?
sec-fc-36.back: us-east-1 (N. Virginia). A certificate for an ALB must be in the same Region as the ALB.

sec-fc-37.back: Origin Access Control: lets only CloudFront read a private S3 bucket via bucket policy; replaces OAI and supports SSE-KMS.

sec-fc-38.back: Signed URL: access to a single file. Signed cookie: access to multiple files without changing URLs.

sec-fc-39.back: GuardDuty: detects threats/anomalous behavior. Inspector: scans EC2/ECR/Lambda for software vulnerabilities. Macie: finds sensitive data (PII) in S3.

sec-fc-40.back: Standard: free, automatic, layer 3/4 DDoS protection. Advanced: paid, 24/7 Shield Response Team, cost protection, enhanced protection.

res-fc-01.front: RDS Multi-AZ DB instance: does the standby serve reads?
res-fc-01.back: No. The standby is only for automatic failover (synchronous replication). To serve reads, use a Read Replica or a Multi-AZ DB cluster (2 readable standbys).

res-fc-02.front: How does Multi-AZ differ from a Read Replica?
res-fc-02.back: Multi-AZ: high availability, synchronous replication, automatic failover, a single endpoint. Read Replica: read scaling, asynchronous replication, its own endpoint, can be cross-Region and must be promoted manually.

res-fc-03.front: How do you keep a web application stateless when scaling horizontally?
res-fc-03.back: Store sessions outside the instance, for example in ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey) or DynamoDB, and store uploaded files in S3 or EFS.

res-fc-04.front: Is a NAT Gateway automatically Multi-AZ?
res-fc-04.back: No. A NAT Gateway is a per-AZ resource; for HA you need one NAT Gateway per AZ, with each AZ route table pointing to the NAT in the same AZ.

res-fc-05.front: How do Local Zones, Wavelength, and Outposts differ?
res-fc-05.back: Local Zones: AWS infrastructure close to major cities for low latency. Wavelength: AWS inside carrier 5G networks. Outposts: AWS racks placed in your own data center.

res-fc-06.front: How many copies of data does Aurora keep?
res-fc-06.back: 6 copies across 3 AZs at the storage layer; up to 15 Aurora Replicas that both serve reads and act as failover targets.

res-fc-07.front: At which layer do ALB, NLB, and GWLB operate?
res-fc-07.back: ALB: layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket). NLB: layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS). GWLB: layer 3, uses GENEVE to insert security appliances.

res-fc-08.front: What do you choose when a load balancer needs a static IP?
res-fc-08.back: NLB (one static IP/Elastic IP per AZ, and an ALB can be placed as its target) or Global Accelerator (2 static anycast IPs). ALB has no static IP.

res-fc-09.back: Lets one HTTPS/TLS listener hold multiple certificates and pick one based on the hostname the client requests. Supported on ALB and NLB, not on CLB.

res-fc-10.front: What is the default deregistration delay?
res-fc-10.back: 300 seconds (configurable 0-3,600 seconds). The LB stops sending new requests to a target being removed but lets in-flight requests finish.

res-fc-11.front: Default cross-zone load balancing on ALB and NLB?
res-fc-11.back: ALB: on by default, no inter-AZ charge. NLB and GWLB: off by default; enabling it incurs inter-AZ data transfer charges.

res-fc-12.front: Can an ALB use Lambda as a target?
res-fc-12.back: Yes. The ALB converts the HTTP request into an event for Lambda; rules let you combine Lambda and EC2 targets on the same ALB.

res-fc-13.front: The ASG does not replace an instance when the application hangs. How do you fix it?
res-fc-13.back: Enable ELB health checks on the Auto Scaling group; by default the ASG only uses EC2 status checks, so it cannot detect application-layer failures.

res-fc-14.back: Keeps a metric (CPU, RequestCountPerTarget...) around a target value; the ASG creates alarms and adjusts automatically. The lowest-operations option.

res-fc-15.front: When do you use scheduled scaling and predictive scaling?
res-fc-15.back: Scheduled: load increases at a known time (cron). Predictive: uses ML on historical data to launch capacity ahead of load with a recurring cycle.

res-fc-16.front: What are lifecycle hooks in an ASG used for?
res-fc-16.back: Pause an instance at Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait to configure it before it receives traffic, or to collect logs/data before it is terminated.

res-fc-17.back: A pool of pre-initialized instances in the Stopped, Running, or Hibernated state, enabling fast scale out for applications with long startup times.

res-fc-18.front: Which metric do you scale SQS workers on?
res-fc-18.back: Backlog per instance = visible messages / InService instances; use target tracking with a target = acceptable latency / processing time per message.

res-fc-19.front: How do SQS Standard and FIFO differ?
res-fc-19.back: Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once, best-effort ordering. FIFO: ordering per message group, exactly-once processing, name ends with .fifo.

res-fc-20.back: How long a message stays hidden after a consumer receives it (default 30 seconds, max 12 hours). If processing takes longer than the timeout, the message reappears and is processed again.

res-fc-21.back: Default 4 days, configurable from 1 minute up to a maximum of 14 days.

res-fc-22.back: Set WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds so ReceiveMessage waits for messages, reducing empty calls, cost, and latency.

res-fc-23.back: A queue that receives messages that were received more than maxReceiveCount times without being processed successfully, for analysis and later redrive.

res-fc-24.back: Publish once to an SNS topic and have multiple SQS queues subscribe, so each system gets its own copy and processes it independently.

res-fc-25.front: When do you choose Amazon MQ instead of SQS/SNS?
res-fc-25.back: When migrating an existing application that uses an ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ broker with standard protocols such as AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, JMS and you do not want to change code.

res-fc-26.front: How does Kinesis Data Streams differ from SQS?
res-fc-26.back: Kinesis lets multiple consumers read the same data, real-time, with replay within retention (24 hours to 365 days). SQS deletes messages after processing and does not support replay.

res-fc-27.back: Maximum 15 minutes per invocation; memory from 128 MB to 10,240 MB (10 GB), with CPU scaling with memory.

res-fc-28.front: How do reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency differ?
res-fc-28.back: Reserved: dedicates and caps concurrency for a function. Provisioned: keeps initialized environments ready to eliminate cold starts (extra cost).

res-fc-29.back: Standard: runs up to 1 year, exactly-once, has execution history. Express: up to 5 minutes, high volume, cheaper for short workloads.

res-fc-30.back: CloudFront Functions: lightweight JavaScript, viewer request/response only, under 1 ms, cheap. Lambda@Edge: Node.js/Python, also origin request/response, has network access, runs longer.

res-fc-31.back: Associates API keys with throttling (rate, burst) and quota per customer; available in REST API.

res-fc-32.back: Alias works at the zone apex, points to AWS resources (ELB, CloudFront, S3 website...), and queries are free. CNAME cannot be used at the zone apex.

res-fc-33.front: How do Geolocation and Latency routing differ?
res-fc-33.back: Geolocation routes by user location (country, continent) for legal/content requirements. Latency routes to the Region with the lowest network latency.

res-fc-34.front: Route 53 health check for a private resource?
res-fc-34.back: The health checkers are outside the VPC and cannot reach it; create a CloudWatch alarm on a metric, then create a health check based on that alarm.

res-fc-35.front: Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints?
res-fc-35.back: Inbound: on-premises resolves names in AWS (private hosted zone). Outbound + forwarding rule: the VPC resolves on-premises domain names.

res-fc-36.back: RPO: the maximum acceptable data loss (measured in time). RTO: the maximum time to restore service after an incident.

res-fc-37.front: How do pilot light and warm standby differ?
res-fc-37.back: Pilot light: only data is replicated; app servers are off or not yet created. Warm standby: the full stack runs at small scale, with shorter RTO and higher cost.

res-fc-38.back: Continuously replicates at block level from on-premises/other clouds/EC2 into a low-cost staging area; RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes, supports drills and failback.

res-fc-39.front: AWS Backup Vault Lock compliance mode
res-fc-39.back: Makes a backup vault WORM: after the grace period, no one (including the root user) can delete backups or remove the lock before retention expires.

res-fc-40.back: An S3 replication option with an SLA of replicating 99.99% of objects within 15 minutes, with metrics and notifications when delayed. Replication requires versioning on both buckets.

res-fc-41.back: A preview of the resources that will be added, modified, or replaced before a stack update; execute only after review.

res-fc-42.back: Detects stack resources that were changed manually outside CloudFormation and no longer match the template configuration.

res-fc-43.back: Deploys the same template to many accounts and Regions; with Organizations (service-managed permissions) it supports automatic deployment to new accounts.

res-fc-44.back: Retain keeps the resource when the stack is deleted; Snapshot takes a final snapshot (EBS, RDS, ElastiCache, Redshift...) and then deletes. The default for most resources is Delete.

res-fc-45.back: The stack reaches CREATE_COMPLETE only when the EC2 instance signals success after cfn-init finishes; on timeout it rolls back.

res-fc-46.front: Beanstalk: Rolling with additional batch vs Immutable
res-fc-46.back: Both keep full capacity. Rolling with additional batch updates existing instances gradually; Immutable builds new instances in a temporary ASG and has the fastest rollback.

res-fc-47.front: SSM Run Command, Patch Manager, State Manager
res-fc-47.back: Run Command: run commands on many nodes without SSH. Patch Manager: patch by baseline in a Maintenance Window. State Manager: keep nodes in a desired state.

res-fc-48.back: Not available by default; install the CloudWatch agent to publish memory/disk metrics, then create a CloudWatch alarm. Detailed monitoring does not add a memory metric.

res-fc-49.front: CloudWatch metric filter vs subscription filter
res-fc-49.back: A metric filter turns log patterns into a metric for alarms; a subscription filter streams logs in real time to Lambda, Kinesis, Firehose.

res-fc-50.back: Distributed tracing with a service map that shows the time and errors in each service to find bottlenecks in microservices.

res-fc-51.back: Admins create a portfolio of approved products (CloudFormation templates); a launch constraint lets users self-launch with the product IAM role, without broad permissions.

res-fc-52.back: A rule in the source account sends events to the event bus of a central account; the target bus needs a resource-based policy allowing the account or organization to send.

res-fc-53.back: Point-to-point connection source (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, MSK, Amazon MQ) → filter → enrichment → target, reducing glue Lambda code.

res-fc-54.back: The task pauses until an external system calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the task token; available only in Standard workflows.

res-fc-55.back: Runs up to 10,000 parallel child executions, reading items directly from S3 to process millions of objects.

res-fc-56.back: Bidirectional no-code data transfer between SaaS (Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Zendesk...) and AWS (S3, Redshift), on a schedule or on events, with filtering and field masking.

perf-fc-01.back: Packs instances close together in 1 AZ for the lowest latency and highest bandwidth between nodes (HPC). The trade-off is a higher risk of correlated failure.

perf-fc-02.front: How many instances does a spread placement group allow?
perf-fc-02.back: At most 7 running instances per AZ per group; each instance is on its own rack to reduce correlated failures.

perf-fc-03.front: What is a partition placement group used for?
perf-fc-03.back: Distributed rack-aware workloads such as HDFS, HBase, Cassandra, Kafka; at most 7 partitions per AZ, each partition is a separate set of racks.

perf-fc-04.back: ENA is the regular enhanced networking (high bandwidth, high PPS). EFA adds OS-bypass for HPC/ML using MPI or NCCL, and supports Linux only.

perf-fc-05.back: An encrypted EBS root volume large enough to hold RAM; RAM is saved to EBS and restored on start, giving a fast startup.

perf-fc-06.front: When does instance store lose data?
perf-fc-06.back: When the instance is stopped, hibernated, or terminated, or the host fails. Data is kept on reboot.

perf-fc-07.back: A service that automatically builds, tests, patches, and distributes AMIs (and container images) through a pipeline, and can share them across Regions/accounts.

perf-fc-08.front: What are the Lambda time and memory limits?
perf-fc-08.back: Up to 15 minutes per invocation, up to 10,240 MB of memory (CPU scales with memory), /tmp up to 10 GB.

perf-fc-09.back: Keeps pre-initialized Lambda environments ready to eliminate cold starts, for predictable load or low-latency requirements.

perf-fc-10.back: ECS when you want simple orchestration with deep AWS integration. EKS when you already use Kubernetes, need Helm/operators, or portability.

perf-fc-11.back: Serverless compute for containers (ECS and EKS): you only declare vCPU/RAM and do not manage EC2. Does not support GPU.

perf-fc-12.back: Manages queues and scheduling of large-scale batch jobs on EC2, Spot, or Fargate; no 15-minute limit like Lambda.

perf-fc-13.back: 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size; IOPS and throughput can be increased independently of size, about 20% cheaper than gp2.

perf-fc-14.back: 3 IOPS per GiB (minimum 100, maximum 16,000); small volumes burst up to 3,000 IOPS. To get more IOPS you must increase size.

perf-fc-15.back: Up to 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MiB/s, 64 TiB per volume, sub-millisecond latency, 99.999% durability.

perf-fc-16.back: io1/io2 only, attaches one volume to up to 16 Nitro instances in the same AZ; needs a cluster-aware file system.

perf-fc-17.front: When to use st1 and sc1?
perf-fc-17.back: HDDs for sequential reads: st1 (up to 500 MiB/s) for big data and logs; sc1 (up to 250 MiB/s) for cold data, the cheapest. Cannot be boot volumes.

perf-fc-18.back: Elastic (scales automatically, pay for use, recommended), Provisioned (reserve throughput up front), Bursting (based on size, uses credits).

perf-fc-19.front: FSx for Lustre scratch vs persistent
perf-fc-19.back: Scratch: temporary, not replicated, cheap, high burst. Persistent: replicated within the AZ, for durable data and long-term processing.

perf-fc-20.back: Multi-protocol file system (NFS, SMB, iSCSI) with snapshots, clones, dedup, SnapMirror; suited to migrating on-prem NetApp.

perf-fc-21.back: At least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD per second per prefix; add prefixes to increase total throughput.

perf-fc-22.back: For files over 5 GB (the single PUT limit). Recommended for files over 100 MB to upload in parallel and retry individual parts.

perf-fc-23.back: Uploads/downloads through an edge location, then over the AWS backbone to a distant bucket; useful when users are far from the bucket Region.

perf-fc-24.back: Single-digit millisecond latency storage class, uses a directory bucket in 1 AZ, placed in the same AZ as compute for ML/analytics.

perf-fc-25.back: Strong read-after-write consistency for all PUT, DELETE, and LIST operations, at no extra charge.

perf-fc-26.back: Read replica: async, readable, used to scale reads. Multi-AZ instance standby: sync, not readable, used only for HA failover.

perf-fc-27.front: What problem does RDS Proxy solve?
perf-fc-27.back: Connection pooling for RDS/Aurora, prevents connection exhaustion (especially from Lambda), reduces failover time, supports IAM auth and Secrets Manager.

perf-fc-28.front: How many copies does Aurora store?
perf-fc-28.back: 6 copies across 3 AZs; writes need 4/6, reads need 3/6; up to 15 Aurora Replicas share the same storage.

perf-fc-29.back: An endpoint pointing to a hand-picked group of instances, for example separating large analytics replicas from the replicas serving the app.

perf-fc-30.front: When should you use Aurora I/O-Optimized?
perf-fc-30.back: When I/O charges are more than about 25% of the Aurora cost; no I/O charges, in exchange for higher instance and storage prices.

perf-fc-31.back: 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read/s (or 2 eventually consistent) for an item up to 4 KB. 1 WCU = 1 write/s for an item up to 1 KB. Transactions cost double.

perf-fc-32.back: GSI: different partition key, can be created any time, eventually consistent only. LSI: same partition key, only created at table creation, supports strongly consistent reads.

perf-fc-33.back: In-memory cache for DynamoDB, reads go from milliseconds down to microseconds, API-compatible; does not speed up writes.

perf-fc-34.back: Lazy loading: caches only on a miss, data can be stale. Write-through: writes to the cache at the same time as the DB, data is always fresh but uses more memory and slows writes. Combine with TTL.

perf-fc-35.back: Redis OSS/Valkey: replication, Multi-AZ, persistence, sorted sets, pub/sub. Memcached: simple, multi-threaded, no replication, no persistence.

perf-fc-36.back: CloudFront caches HTTP/HTTPS content at the edge. Global Accelerator provides 2 static anycast IPs, supports TCP/UDP, does not cache, and offers fast multi-Region failover.

perf-fc-37.back: A primary/secondary origin pair; when the primary returns a configured error code (for example 5xx) or times out, CloudFront switches to the secondary for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS.

perf-fc-38.back: Each shard: writes 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s, reads 2 MB/s (shared); enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own 2 MB/s.

perf-fc-39.back: The new name of Kinesis Data Firehose: delivers streaming data near real-time to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, HTTP; transform with Lambda, convert to Parquet/ORC.

perf-fc-40.front: How much data can 1 Gbps transfer per day?
perf-fc-40.back: About 125 MB/s, or about 10.8 TB/day at 100% bandwidth utilization; 100 TB takes about 9-10 days.

perf-fc-41.front: SageMaker AI vs ready-made AI services
perf-fc-41.back: SageMaker AI: build/train/deploy your own model (notebooks, training jobs, endpoints). AI services (Rekognition, Textract...): call an API, no ML experts needed, least operational overhead.

perf-fc-42.back: Serverless API access to foundation models; Knowledge Bases (RAG over documents), Agents, Guardrails, fine-tuning. Customer data is not used to train the base models.

perf-fc-43.back: Textract: extracts text, forms (key-value), and tables from scanned documents/PDFs, invoices, ID documents. Rekognition: short text in natural images such as signs and license plates.

perf-fc-44.back: Image/video analysis: objects, scenes, faces (comparison, search), celebrities, content moderation, PPE; Custom Labels for your own labels.

perf-fc-45.back: NLP: sentiment, entities, key phrases, language detection, PII detection/redaction, custom classification. Comprehend Medical for medical information and PHI.

perf-fc-46.back: Transcribe: speech to text (call recordings, subtitles, PII redaction). Polly: text to speech (read articles aloud, neural voices, SSML).

perf-fc-47.back: Lex: voice/text chatbot engine (intents, slots, Lambda). Connect: cloud contact center that can integrate Lex as a self-service bot.

perf-fc-48.back: Kendra: natural-language search over internal documents. Personalize: real-time product recommendations. Q Business: AI assistant over enterprise data; Q Developer: coding assistant.

cost-fc-01.front: How much cheaper is a Spot Instance, and how much warning do you get before it is reclaimed?
cost-fc-01.back: Up to about 90% cheaper than On-Demand; AWS gives a 2-minute warning via instance metadata and EventBridge before reclaiming.

cost-fc-02.front: What do Compute Savings Plans apply to?
cost-fc-02.back: EC2 in any family, size, OS, tenancy, and Region, plus AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda. Most flexible, discount up to about 66%.

cost-fc-03.front: How do EC2 Instance Savings Plans differ from Compute Savings Plans?
cost-fc-03.back: EC2 Instance SP is tied to one instance family in one Region, with a deeper discount (up to about 72%), but does not apply to Fargate/Lambda and cannot change Region.

cost-fc-04.back: Standard RI has a deeper discount and can be sold on the RI Marketplace, but cannot change family/OS. Convertible RI has a smaller discount but can change family, OS, and tenancy.

cost-fc-05.front: Does a Regional RI reserve capacity?
cost-fc-05.back: No. A Regional RI only discounts usage in every AZ in the Region. To reserve capacity you need a Zonal RI or an On-Demand Capacity Reservation.

cost-fc-06.back: Reserves EC2 capacity in one specific AZ, no term commitment, billed even when no instance is running. Combine with Savings Plans/Regional RI to get a discount.

cost-fc-07.front: License per socket/core (BYOL) → what to choose?
cost-fc-07.back: Dedicated Hosts: they expose sockets, cores, and host ID and support host affinity. Dedicated Instances do not qualify because they do not expose the physical hardware.

cost-fc-08.front: Baseline must always run but spikes must be cheap → which architecture?
cost-fc-08.back: An Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy: On-Demand base capacity (covered by Savings Plans) and Spot for capacity above the base.

cost-fc-09.back: priceCapacityOptimized: picks the pools least likely to be interrupted while still low in price; combine multiple instance types to diversify.

cost-fc-10.back: Uses ML on CloudWatch metrics to recommend right-sizing for EC2, ASG, EBS, Lambda, ECS Fargate, RDS. Memory metrics require the CloudWatch agent.

cost-fc-11.front: Minimum storage duration of Standard-IA, Glacier IR, Glacier Flexible, Deep Archive
cost-fc-11.back: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: 30 days; Glacier Instant Retrieval and Flexible Retrieval: 90 days; Deep Archive: 180 days.

cost-fc-12.back: Expedited 1–5 minutes, Standard 3–5 hours, Bulk 5–12 hours (Bulk retrieval is free).

cost-fc-13.front: How long does Glacier Deep Archive retrieval take?
cost-fc-13.back: Standard within 12 hours, Bulk within 48 hours. No Expedited. Cheapest for 7–10 year archives.

cost-fc-14.front: "Unknown or changing access patterns" on S3
cost-fc-14.back: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: moves tiers automatically, no retrieval fee, only a small per-object monitoring fee.

cost-fc-15.front: When to use S3 One Zone-IA?
cost-fc-15.back: Infrequently accessed data that can be re-created (thumbnails, secondary copies). Only 1 AZ, about 20% cheaper than Standard-IA.

cost-fc-16.front: When is S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval a good fit?
cost-fc-16.back: Archive data accessed about once a quarter but needed in milliseconds; cheaper storage than Standard-IA, 90-day minimum.

cost-fc-17.back: The (authenticated) requester pays for requests and data transfer; the bucket owner pays only for storage.

cost-fc-18.front: S3 Storage Lens vs S3 Inventory
cost-fc-18.back: Storage Lens: organization-level usage/activity dashboard and cost recommendations. Inventory: periodic file listing of objects and metadata (CSV/ORC/Parquet).

cost-fc-19.front: Bucket with Versioning enabled has bloated costs → what to do?
cost-fc-19.back: Add lifecycle rules to expire noncurrent versions and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload.

cost-fc-20.front: What can AWS Budgets actions do?
cost-fc-20.back: When a threshold is exceeded: apply an IAM policy, apply an SCP, or stop EC2/RDS instances; run automatically or wait for approval.

cost-fc-21.front: What are Cost and Usage Report / Data Exports used for?
cost-fc-21.back: Export the most detailed billing data (hourly, per resource, with tags) to S3 as CUR 2.0 or FOCUS; analyze with Athena/QuickSight.

cost-fc-22.front: Tag applied but not visible in Cost Explorer?
cost-fc-22.back: You must activate the tag as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console of the management account; it is not retroactive.

cost-fc-23.front: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection vs AWS Budgets
cost-fc-23.back: Anomaly Detection uses ML to detect unusual spend, no threshold needed. Budgets alert on fixed thresholds you set.

cost-fc-24.back: One bill, combined usage to reach lower pricing tiers, RIs and Savings Plans shared across accounts; no extra charge.

cost-fc-25.front: Which support plan is needed for the full Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks?
cost-fc-25.back: Business Support or higher (Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, Enterprise). Basic/Developer get only the core checks.

cost-fc-26.back: Creates a pro forma bill with custom pricing for showback/chargeback or resellers; does not change the real AWS bill.

cost-fc-27.back: Inbound from the internet, traffic within the same AZ over private IP, and from an AWS origin (S3, EC2, ALB) to CloudFront.

cost-fc-28.front: Private EC2 reads S3 heavily, NAT Gateway charges are high → solution?
cost-fc-28.back: Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 (and DynamoDB): free, you only add a route to the route table.

cost-fc-29.front: Is an Interface VPC endpoint free?
cost-fc-29.back: No. Charged per hour per AZ and per GB processed. Only Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free.

cost-fc-30.front: What changed with public IPv4 charges in Feb 2024?
cost-fc-30.back: Every public IPv4 address is charged hourly, including attached Elastic IPs. Reduce by dropping public IPs, using IPv6, endpoints, Session Manager.

cost-fc-31.back: gp3 is about 20% cheaper per GB, with a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of size; convert with Elastic Volumes without downtime.

cost-fc-32.back: On-demand: pay per request, for unpredictable load/lots of idle time. Provisioned + Auto Scaling (+ reserved capacity): cheaper for steady load.

cost-fc-33.front: When is Aurora Serverless v2 a good fit?
cost-fc-33.back: Variable or intermittent database load, dev/test; scales by ACU, can be configured with min 0 ACU to auto-pause when idle.

cost-fc-34.back: An AWS solution that automatically starts/stops EC2 and RDS on a schedule based on tags, cutting off-hours dev/test environment costs.

cost-fc-35.front: Does increasing Lambda memory always increase cost?
cost-fc-35.back: No. CPU is proportional to memory, so a shorter run time can lower the total cost; use Lambda Power Tuning to find the optimum.

cost-fc-36.back: Reduce data scanned: partition data, use compressed columnar formats Parquet/ORC, combine small files.

cost-fc-37.back: Serverless is billed per RPU-hour while queries run, for sporadic load. Provisioned + reserved nodes is cheaper for always-on warehouses.

cost-fc-38.front: FSx for Lustre scratch vs persistent
cost-fc-38.back: Scratch is cheap, no replication, for short-term temporary processing; persistent is for long-term storage with replication. Both can link to S3.

cost-fc-39.front: When to choose Snowball Edge over network transfer?
cost-fc-39.back: When a network transfer would take too long (several weeks or more) or saturate bandwidth, for many TB to PB of data moved once.

cost-fc-40.front: EBS vs EFS: how is capacity billed?
cost-fc-40.back: EBS is billed on provisioned capacity whether used or not; EFS is billed on actual used capacity but at a higher price per GB, reduced with lifecycle to IA/Archive.

cost-fc-41.front: When is Lambda cheaper than EC2/ECS, and when is it the opposite?
cost-fc-41.back: Lambda is cheap for sparse, spiky load with lots of idle time because idle costs nothing. For high, steady 24/7 load, EC2 or ECS on EC2 with Savings Plans is usually cheaper.

cost-fc-42.back: Runs Fargate tasks on spare capacity at up to about 70% off; reclaimed with a 2-minute warning (SIGTERM). Does not support Windows or ARM64 tasks.

cost-fc-43.front: Capacity provider strategy: base and weight
cost-fc-43.back: base is the minimum number of tasks always placed on one provider (e.g. FARGATE base 2); weight splits the rest between providers (e.g. FARGATE:FARGATE_SPOT = 1:3).

cost-fc-44.back: Diversify across many instance types and AZs (or attribute-based selection) and use the price-capacity-optimized/capacity-optimized allocation strategy. Raising the max price does not help.

cost-fc-45.front: Spot workers that do not lose work when reclaimed
cost-fc-45.back: Pull work from SQS and delete the message only after processing (it reappears after the visibility timeout); checkpoint progress to S3/DynamoDB to resume.

cost-fc-46.back: EC2 (families with a g), Lambda arm64, Fargate ARM64, RDS/Aurora, ElastiCache, OpenSearch. Better price/performance than x86; needs ARM64-compatible code/images.

cost-fc-47.front: Lambda billed while waiting for an external API: solution?
cost-fc-47.back: Move the waiting to Step Functions (Wait state or callback task token); Standard workflows are billed per state transition, not for waiting time.

cost-fc-48.back: Batch has no extra charge; use a Spot compute environment with SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED, many instance types, and a retry strategy for interrupted jobs.

cost-fc-49.front: Which data transfer flows are free?
cost-fc-49.back: Inbound from the internet; within the same AZ over private IP; EC2 ↔ S3/DynamoDB in the same Region (not via NAT); AWS origin → CloudFront; RDS/Aurora Multi-AZ replication.

cost-fc-50.front: Gateway endpoint vs interface endpoint: cost
cost-fc-50.back: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB only) are free. Interface endpoints charge hourly per AZ + per GB, but the processing fee is lower than a NAT Gateway.

cost-fc-51.front: One NAT per AZ or one shared NAT?
cost-fc-51.back: One NAT per AZ: HA, no cross-AZ fees, but more hourly fees (for production). One shared NAT: lower hourly cost but cross-AZ fees and a single point of failure (acceptable for dev/test).

cost-fc-52.back: All, 200, 100. Price Class 100 uses only edges in the cheapest areas (North America, Europe): cheaper but higher latency for users elsewhere.

cost-fc-53.front: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway: cost
cost-fc-53.back: Peering has no hourly or processing fee and same-AZ traffic is free, but it is not transitive. TGW charges per attachment-hour + per GB processed, in exchange for easy hub-and-spoke management.

cost-fc-54.front: Direct Connect vs Site-to-Site VPN: cost
cost-fc-54.back: VPN: hourly fee per connection + egress at internet rates, cheap for low volume, quick to set up. Direct Connect: fixed port fee + cheaper egress, worthwhile for large steady volumes.

cost-fc-55.front: Cross-zone load balancing and inter-AZ fees
cost-fc-55.back: NLB/GWLB have cross-zone off by default; turning it on incurs inter-AZ fees. ALB always has cross-zone on and does not charge inter-AZ for it.

cost-fc-56.back: Cost Explorer grouped by usage type (DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, NatGateway-Bytes, DataTransfer-Out-Bytes); CUR + Athena per resource; VPC Flow Logs for source/destination pairs.
